# Introduction

Literacy provides the base skillset of all student education, both through a student’s school years as well as beyond. In 2012, the Annie E. Casey Foundation published research on the importance of early literacy skills and poverty rates. Students who have not met expected standards in literacy by 3^rd^ grade will quickly fall behind, risking even their likelihood of graduation from high school [@Hernandez2011]. Yet programs designed to build literacy skills in childhood are often at risk.

In Washington state, budget cuts from the state Legislature recently eliminated the Imagination Library program, an early learning program providing books for children from birth to age 5 [@Lotmore2025]. The Office of the Superintendent of Public Education (OSPI) has stepped in with discretionary funds for the current school year (2025-26), but the future of the program in Washington state remains unclear.

Literacy itself has a broad definition and can include word decoding, reading speed, text comprehension, reading strategies, and even motivation [@Jackson2005; @Talwar2022]. At its core, though, are the skills of reading, reading comprehension, and writing. At the secondary school level, Washington state uses standardized tests provided by the Smarter Balanced Assessment Consortium (SBAC) to track student achievement in English Language Arts (ELA) and Mathematics. Tests can be administered as many as eight times in a student’s secondary schooling, from grades 3 to 11.

These test scores provide a thread throughout secondary schooling where we can track the rate at which students are achieving expected literacy goals. At the same time, they measure the success of teaching and learning programs implemented within the schools and school districts. In fact, standardized tests are a direct result of the No Child Left Behind (NCLB) and Every Student Succeeds Act (ESSA) implemented by the Bush and Obama administrations in 2002 and 2015 respectively.

Although student success can be represented in many ways, including steady employment or military enrollment, 4-year college enrollment is a well-measured indicator of post-secondary outcomes.  According to the Education Research & Data Center (ERDC) for Washington State, the rate of enrollment in 4-year colleges has remained nearly flat over the past 10 years, while enrollment in 2-year colleges and technical schools has decreased by four percentage points. At the same time, ERDC reports rates of enrollment in college-prep English courses has dropped from 9% to 6% for 4-year college destined students and from 36% to 15% for students expecting to enter 2-year colleges or technical schools [@ERDC2026].

With the decrease in enrollment, the Washington Student Achievement Council (WSAC) has set a goal that "70 percent of adults ages 25 to 44 should earn a post-secondary credential" [@WSAC2026Plan]. In the 10 years ending in 2024, though, WSAC measured an 18% decrease in post-secondary enrollment [@WSAC2026Dashboard].

This paper seeks to understand the relationship between student achievement in literacy at the school district level, and outcomes of that achievement in post-secondary success. Specifically, I will be assessing the relationship between ELA scores on SBAC testing and enrollment in 4-year colleges. With literacy capability in secondary school strongly associated with college readiness, tracking literacy achievement through SBAC scores may be a strong indication of college enrollment.

# Background

## Literacy in Secondary Education

Research has long established a close relationship between literacy and academic success. Most recent discussions emphasize the link between early literacy and secondary education, notably high school graduation. Third-grade is frequently identified as a key point for reading skills in determining not just success, but graduation from high school. As much as 16% of children without proficient reading skills after third grade fail to graduate from high school on time, a statistic exacerbated further by a student’s socioeconomic status [@Hernandez2011].

Although difficult to examine the direct impact of early literacy programs on student reading capability, we can examine student results through standardized testing. Comprehensive programs prior to third grade show substantial increases in reading scores on standardized tests used by states for evaluating outcomes [@Westall2023]. Further, evidence indicates the impact of those literacy programs also spills over to Math scores [@Westall2023].

The topic is hardly unique to the United States or the English language. A 2014 study based in Spain identified student literacy, again through standardized testing and found that reading skills and reading comprehension capability measured in earlier grades affects outcomes of later grades. Students in late primary (fifth and sixth grades) and early secondary (i.e. high school) grades showed natural improvement in reading comprehension with age, but those with reading difficulties in earlier grades continued to show weaker results in later grades [@Fidalgo2014]. Similarly, research in Finland found that reading and spelling capability assessed at the end of primary school (9^th^ grade) predicted secondary school choices, tracking students into either general education (a college-bound track) or vocational education [@Savolainen2008]. The assessment of literacy skills in earlier grades (i.e. US secondary school) ultimately predicts college enrollment and post-secondary outcomes.

Although much has been examined regarding early literacy programs, less has been said about the response to those students that perform poorly on standardized tests. Based on standardized test scores, students in Florida required to enroll in remedial reading courses in high school are 5.4% less likely to enroll in either a 2-year or 4-year college program [@Ozek2025]. An unfortunate side effect of early assignment to a remedial course is that students can get “tracked” in remedial courses in general, resulting in fewer opportunities to succeed elsewhere in their education.

## Literacy in College

The link between secondary school literacy skills and post-secondary outcomes continues in more recent research in the US. “\[Adults\] with a history of reading disability \[are\] less likely to pursue further education and more likely to spend a significant time in unemployment” [@James2024]. More directly, students with weak reading comprehension skills show lower scores on SATs, test results often used to determine college enrollment. Interestingly, reading comprehension weaknesses have a more pronounced impact on math and science test results than in ELA results [@James2024]. Despite the clear impact of literacy skills on student outcomes both in high school and beyond, there is evidence that colleges have set aside the need for literacy standards for student acceptance.

A 2010 comparison of the reading comprehension of first-year university students at the University of Prince Edward Island to the broader population of Canada, found no difference in skills. The implication is that literacy skills were not relevant to college enrollment [@Graham2010]. Five years earlier, a study of nearly 200 students at the University of Iowa found no strong relationship between literacy skills and academic success [@Jackson2005]. The question is, then, how important are reading and reading comprehension skills to college enrollment and college success?

In response to these earlier studies citing a lack of importance, we need to consider the student population participating in the research. The University of Iowa student population was restricted to second and third year students in a single educational psychology class. The authors themselves describe them as “mature, successful students” [@Jackson2005], thus nullifying the analysis as to whether their literacy skills lead to academic success. Similarly, the research in Canada was limited to just over 220 students attending a single university in Eastern Canada. Limited samples prevent a definitive answer on the importance of literacy of secondary school students and their post-secondary opportunities.

This brings into question, are reading comprehension scores on standardized tests valid for assessing whether students are ready for college? Instead of depending on this assessment of reading skills to measure readiness, can we instead bring them up to a level of readiness to ensure success? Students entering college without the requisite literacy skills are often required to enroll in developmental or remedial reading courses as part of their first term. Completing such courses proves beneficial, as those students, previously unprepared, went on to complete college at the same rate as their peers [@Cox2003].

## Standardized Testing and Long-Term Outcomes

A common thread to the assessment of student literacy at all levels is the development and application of standardized tests of reading and reading comprehension. Though standardized testing is hardly new, increased attention in the United States started with the No Child Left Behind (NCLB) act in 2002 implemented by Bush administration. NCLB was updated in 2015 as the Every Student Succeeds Act (ESSA) by the Obama administration. A key requirement of ESSA (and NCLB before it) was the implementation of standardized testing for reading and math in grades 3 through 8, and at least once in high school [@us_congress_essa_2015].

Research relating standardized test results to college enrollment has primarily emphasized college acceptance tests like the ACT and SAT. An extensive literature review in 2013 sought to understand the most relevant predictors of student success across elementary, middle, and high school. Literacy in third grade is correlated with ELA standardized tests results (ACT) in middle grades, which are in-turn related to enrollment in honors and dual-credit courses. [@Hein2013]. Those advanced courses, e.g. Advanced Placement (AP) and International Baccalaureate (IB) are subsequently correlated with college enrollment.

As discussed previously, weaknesses in literacy skills impact not just ELA test scores on, for example, the SAT, but can have a larger impact on Science and Math scores [@James2024].  But with universities waving the requirement for college entrance exams over the past five years, these tests may no longer have relevance in assessing college readiness for students. An overall GPA may hide weaknesses in a specific subject. Further, students pursuing 2-year or Community and Technical Colleges (CTC) may slip through without recognition of literacy deficiencies.

Perhaps there is no stronger argument for the importance of literacy skills to success in college than in a 2022 article by Amani Talwar et. al. “In the current landscape of higher education, academic reading tasks are important components of college courses and performance over time.” And further: “it is likely that many of the factors that contribute to academic reading performance are also predictive of general academic success in college” [@Talwar2022]. This research team chose to develop their own series of tests to apply to test subjects due to the potential skewing of the testing population. Outcomes of their research indicate vocabulary and reading comprehension, commonly evaluated in standardized tests, as important skills for predicting early college success.

With the wealth of evidence, standardized assessments demonstrate a clear connection to post-secondary success, specifically enrollment in 2-year and 4-year colleges. However, those assessments examined occur most often toward the end of a student’s secondary school studies. SAT and ACT scores are specifically designed for college entrance assessment, and will have, by design, a skewed student population already seeking college. Similarly, AP scores and similar dual-credit courses occur most often in the last two years of secondary school, also attracting students already targeting college.

SAT, ACT, and AP testing students are, by nature, preparing for these standardized tests. In fact, AP courses are designed specifically for preparing students to take AP courses. The tests themselves are designed specifically as an assessment of college readiness [@Talwar2022].

If we are to increase college enrollment to 70% of the adult population, as WSAC has targeted, we need to seek opportunities beyond the self-selected college bound population. In Washington state, the SBAC tests are not subject to the focus of test-taking strategies like the SAT or ACT might be. Most students are given the SBAC simply as part of the expected school year. They do not study or prepare for the test outside of "teaching to the test" strategies that may occur as part of the standard school curriculum. However, those strategies would be applied equally across all students. Compare this to an AP course, for example, where a select number of students are choosing to take a course centered on the subject matter of the AP exam.

## Annual Standardized Test Scores in College Enrollment

\<Purpose of the paper:\> This paper examines the results of standardized tests given to secondary school students in Washington state on an annual basis. SBAC test results in ELA and Math have the advantage of already being implemented as part of ESSA federal requirements, being applied across the entire student population (with exceptions for students with learning disabilities), &&&

\<What I will do:\> &&&

\<Why it is relevant:\> By demonstrating the relevance of existing annualized testing on college enrollment, state and district educational organizations can use the information to more directly understand where gaps exist in literacy achievement and apply critical funding as appropriate. Increased enrollment in secondary education can only occur with a clear picture of where schools and school districts are not driving enrollment. &&&

# Data and Methodology

Washington student achievement on SBAC test results, along with enrollment in college, are reported as ratios through the Washington State Open Data Portal (<https://data.wa.gov>) and through online dashboards provided by ERDC. Through regression analysis, I will analyze SBAC test results in respect to college enrollment rates for students at individual high schools or across school districts. A possible secondary question I am considering is whether SBAC ELA scores are more relevant to post-secondary enrollment than SBAC Math scores.

Due to student privacy, data is not available at the individual student level, and I will be working with overall rates of enrollment and rates of meeting test standards at the school and school district level. This introduces a potential risk of an ecological fallacy. During the project, I will consider leveraging socioeconomic factors including income level and ethnicity to control for potential issues.

Additionally, SBAC scores from a single year (e.g. 11^th^ grade) may not be wholly representative of student achievement and readiness. To validate the robustness of the relationship between SBAC achievement scores and post-secondary enrollment, I intend to analyze multiple perspectives of standardized test scores:

-   Most recent SBAC scores (last score reported in a school district).

-   Last two SBAC scores to smooth single test variations.

-   A simple aggregation of SBAC scores across all grades in a school district.

-   Weighted scores across all grades emphasizing later grades over earlier.

Aggregated and weighted scores across grade levels will be measured and analyzed at a school district level.

I am making a deliberate choice to filter assessment data to All Students, Female, and Low-Income. Non-Low Income is assumed as (1 - Low Income). Male is assumed as (1 - Female). This does negate Gender X, or groups it as Male. However, the overall percentage of students identifying as Gender X in assessments is &&&.

It should be noted that we are not measuring students. We are measuring Districts. A student, for instance, has scores that change over time, culminating, usually, in a final score in 10th or 11th grade. If we were measuring students, we would need to account for the last time a student completed an SBAC and when they enrolled in college, which can be separated by 1 or 2 years. However, in the case of this analysis, we are measuring the overall performance of a District in a given year. This is compared to the college enrollment rates of that District. With SBAC assessments used as a District level score, we can compare the District assessment results to the District enrollment rates without concern for the difference in time between a student graudating and a student enrolling.

## Methodology

I will be tracking the rates at which students are:

-   Entering college (2-year or 4-year)

-   Control factor: Participating in remedial courses in the first year. Theoretically this is an indication that the student is NOT ready for college.

This will be measured based on influencing variables such as:

-   Rate at which students meet standards for ELA testing.

-   Rate at which test results within a District change over time.

There are many factors that can influence a child's readiness for reading and writing throughout their schooling, including income levels, environment (e.g. urban vs. rural), gender, and ethnicity. For the purpose of this project, I will attempt to control for low-income status and gender, though recognize that additional factors may be hidden in the data. My goal is to assess how reading & writing ability, as measured through standardized testing, predict enrollment in 4-year colleges. Math scores will also be considered as a contributing factor to enrollment rates.

My primary assessment of literacy capability will be based on the percent of students meeting expected standards for the ELA SBAC test. This test is administered 8 times throughout a student's secondary school education. The OSPI data includes the total number of students testing, the total number meeting standards, and the percent meeting standards. An SBAC score is a value of 1 to 4, with values of 3 and 4 indicating the student met expected standards.

The data includes multiple school years and grade levels. However, as this research question does not examine changes across time, district level results are aggregated into a single indicator for the district.

The OSPI data includes scores for individual schools and for each grade, indicating the percent of students meeting expectations within the grade for that school year. Aggregates are also provided at the All Grades level and at the school district level. I have chosen to create an aggregate score for each school year and for each school district based on the percentages provided for all grades and all schools within the district. This is handled using a Logit transformation of weighted scores. I am weighting the grades so that later grades have more influence on the overall literacy score, indicating more influence on college enrollment and persistence.

$$ \text{logit}_{g} = \ln\!\left(\frac{p_{g}}{1 - p_{g}}\right) $$

$$ w_{g} = \text{grade\_weight}_{g} \cdot n_{g} $$

$$ \text{WeightedLogit}_{d,y} = \frac{ \sum_{g} \left( \text{logit}_{g} \cdot w_{g} \right) }{ \sum_{g} w_{g} } $$

Above are formulas rendered in Latex

Enrollment rates for each year are aggregated at the School District level using a Logit_average technique. I did not have access to the underlying numbers for students enrolled in each year. Thus, the ratios provided in my source data needed to be averaged without weighting. The Logit-average technique is appropriate for averaging ratios.

Formulas:

Logit-average formula converts each rate of enrollment into a logit value using the natural logarithm. Values across years are averaged.

$$
\text{LogitAvg} 
= \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \operatorname{logit}(r_t)
$$

Once the values are averaged, the value is converted back into a standard ratio value.

$$
R = \operatorname{logistic}(\text{LogitAvg})
= \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\text{LogitAvg}}}
$$

```{r}
#| label: fig1

#  geom_point() +
#  xlab("Weight (in thousands of lbs)") + 
#  ylab("Miles per Gallon")
dfPlot <- read_rds("rds/scatter_matrix.rds")

ggplot(dfPlot, aes(x = x_value, y = percent_enrolled)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE,
              linewidth = 0.4, color = "steelblue") +
  facet_grid(enrollment_level ~ predictor, 
             scales = "free_x",
             switch = "y") +
  labs(
    title = "Percent Enrolled vs. ELA Score",
    x = "ELA Score",
    y = "Enrollment Rate"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "gray90"),
    strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, face = "bold")
  )

```
